turns.doctor_question: Hello, welcome. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, doctor, thank you for fitting me in. I guess the main thing, the thing that finally made me pick up the phone and make this appointment—which, honestly, my wife has been telling me to do for a good long while now—is just this... this constant feeling I get. It’s hard to explain exactly, but it’s like I’ve got this motor, you know? Just humming right under my skin. It really acts up whenever I’m supposed to just sit down and be still. 

Like, at work. I'm a building cleaner, so normally I'm on my feet sweeping, mopping, taking out the recycling, which is great for me, I like being active. But every Tuesday they have these mandatory staff meetings. They cram us all into this little break room with those terrible plastic chairs, and within five minutes, I swear, my whole body is just vibrating. I start shifting around in my seat, adjusting my posture, crossing my legs, uncrossing them... 

And it’s not just work, either. We have these church event briefings on the weekends because I help out with the volunteer crew, setting up the folding tables and whatnot for the congregation. The coordinator will be going over the schedule, just talking and talking, and I’m sitting there feeling like I'm going to literally jump out of my own skin. I almost always end up having to stand up and lean against the wall in the back of the room, or I'll just find some excuse to go check on the coffee urns or take the trash out early just so I can move my legs. I just can't seem to stay put.

symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient describes squirming and shifting around in their seat, constantly adjusting posture and crossing/uncrossing legs during meetings.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient reports frequently standing up or finding excuses to leave their seat during mandatory meetings and briefings where sitting is expected.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient explicitly describes an intense internal restlessness, feeling like they might 'jump out of my own skin' when required to sit still.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient uses the classic description of feeling like they have a 'motor humming right under my skin' that drives their constant need to move.

turns.doctor_question: Did you experience this same kind of restlessness and difficulty sitting still when you were a child?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, boy, did I ever. It’s funny you ask that, because my wife and I were just talking about this the other day when we were going through some old boxes in the attic, finding some of my old report cards. But yes, absolutely. I mean, going all the way back to grade school, I was always, always getting into trouble for it. 

I can still picture those old wooden desks with the metal legs, you know the ones? They had the little cubby inside for your books and the groove on top for your pencil. I could never just stay put in mine. I was constantly popping out of my seat. The teacher would be up at the chalkboard, and I'd just be up, wandering over to the pencil sharpener or going to look at the class pet or whatever. 

And it wasn't just the sitting, it was... well, I was always talking over the teacher, too. They’d be in the middle of a lesson, explaining long division or history or something, and a thought would just pop into my head and I’d blurt it right out. I just couldn't hold it in, it felt like the words were burning a hole in my tongue. Or, oh, this used to drive them absolutely crazy—they'd hand out a worksheet or a test, and before they even finished giving the directions to the class, I was already rushing ahead, scribbling away, trying to get it done. Half the time I’d do the whole thing wrong because I didn't wait to hear the actual instructions, I just saw the paper and went for it. 

My mother, God rest her soul, she used to get these notes sent home from the teachers all the time. She had this saying for me... she used to say I acted like I was "wound too tight." Like one of those little tin toy cars where you turn the key on the side until it can't turn anymore, and then you let it go and it just zips all over the kitchen floor crashing into the baseboards. That's exactly how she described me, even as a little kid. Just wound completely tight and ready to spring. So, yeah, it's definitely not a new thing, it's just... I guess it's just never really stopped, you know? Even now, like I was saying about those Tuesday staff meetings, it's that exact same feeling I had when I was eight years old.

symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient describes rushing ahead on worksheets and doing them wrong because he did not wait to hear or follow the actual instructions.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient explicitly states he could never stay put and was 'constantly popping out of my seat' to wander around the classroom.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient confirms the doctor's question about childhood restlessness and describes wandering around the classroom inappropriately.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient's mother described him as being 'wound too tight' and like a wind-up toy car that 'zips all over,' indicating he acted as if driven by a motor.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient admits that a thought would pop into his head and he would 'blurt it right out' during lessons.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient mentions that he was 'always talking over the teacher,' demonstrating interrupting and intruding on others.

turns.doctor_question: Aside from being physically restless, do you also struggle with staying focused or getting easily distracted during tasks?
turns.patient_response:
Focus? No, not really. I mean, I don't think so. It's not like my mind wanders off to a million different places or I forget what I'm doing in the middle of doing it. Actually, when I'm working, I'm pretty dialed in. 

Like, take my route at the building. When I'm doing the floors on the third level—which is mostly the executive suites, so they expect it to be absolutely spotless—there's this whole method I have, you know? First, I do the dry sweep, making sure I get my broom right up under the baseboards and behind those heavy oak filing cabinets they have in the corner offices. Then I come through with the wet mop, doing these tight figure-eights so I don't leave any streaks on the tile. I can stay completely focused on that for hours. It's almost like a rhythm, just sweeping, mopping, emptying the bins. 

My wife actually says I get tunnel vision sometimes when I'm working on a project. Just last weekend, the lawnmower was acting up, sputtering and blowing black smoke, so I took the carburetor apart on my workbench in the garage. I must have stood there for three straight hours, just scrubbing every little valve and jet with a wire brush and some carb cleaner, and I didn't look up once. I was totally zeroed in. 

So, no, it's not like my brain is flying away like a bird or I'm getting distracted by every little shiny thing that catches my eye. I know exactly what I need to do, and my mind is right there on the job. It's really just... it's the sitting part, like I was saying before. If my hands and feet are moving, if I'm engaged physically, my brain is locked in tight. It's only when they make me stop moving, like in those awful staff meetings, that the motor starts revving and I feel like I'm gonna explode. So yeah, staying on task or paying attention? That's never really been the problem for me, as long as the task lets me stay on my feet.

symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient describes feeling like they are going to explode when forced to sit still, indicating severe internal restlessness.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient explicitly uses the phrase 'the motor starts revving' to describe their need for constant physical engagement.
symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient explicitly denies having trouble staying focused, stating they can stay completely focused on tasks for hours.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient denies being easily distracted, stating their mind does not wander and they don't get distracted by shiny things.
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient denies forgetting what they are doing in the middle of a task.
